headline: Nvidia's CEO admits an affair with a suspected spy.
summary: Jensen Huang, who runs the chipmaker Nvidia, told his staff Sunday he was unfaithful to his wife. US intelligence officials believe the woman was a Chinese spy sent to get him pushing for chip sales to China. Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation and says it has no reason to think secrets leaked. He stays CEO.

cover_question.q: Why would China spy on him?

cover_answer: To get him to lobby for selling Nvidia's chips to China.
table_question: How would you know if a new friend only wanted your secrets?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The man who runs the company that makes the tiny chips inside computers got close to a woman who may have been a spy. A spy tries to get secrets, like someone peeking at your cards in a game. He said sorry to everyone at his company, and the grown-ups are checking whether any secrets got out. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: The peek at the cards carries it, and the affair stays unnamed. At six one vivid detail stands for the whole event, so the detail is the cards.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and reads your face before your words, so the script hands them a card game and a sorry, and the affair stays out. Expect "did he get in trouble?" He said sorry to his whole company, and the board is checking. He still has his job for now.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Nvidia makes the chips that run AI, and US rules limit which ones China can buy. US officials say China sent a spy to get close to Nvidia's boss so he'd push to sell them anyway. On Sunday Jensen Huang admitted a relationship with her and said sorry. The board hired outside lawyers, a referee checking the replay.
8-12.why: A rule, a way around it, a check: a chain they can follow at eight.
8-12.why_long: An eight-year-old is working out cause and effect and whether adults get held to the rules, so the script runs the chain: a rule on chip sales, a spy sent around it, a boss who said sorry, a board that hired outside lawyers. The referee is the check. Expect "will he get fired?" Not so far. The board says it backs him.

13-17.script: If the world's most powerful CEO can be targeted by a spy, who can't be? Jensen Huang admitted an affair with a woman US intelligence says China sent to get him lobbying for chip sales. Second: Nvidia called her a normal business contact for weeks, then hired lawyers. Which Nvidia do you trust?
13-17.why: The company denied it, then investigated. At 13 they can weigh both.
13-17.why_long: A 13-year-old can hold two true things at once, so the script gives both: a company that called her a routine contact for weeks, and a board that then hired outside lawyers. Asking which Nvidia to believe is practice at weighing a source against its record. Expect "did Trump know?" He was briefed in October, Axios reports.

5-7.a: Someone who acts like a friend to learn secrets for another country.

8-12.q: Why would China spy on him?
8-12.a: His chips run AI. China wants them, and US rules limit the sale.
Nobody knows yet. The board says it has no reason to think so.

13-17.q: Why does this matter beyond his marriage?
13-17.a: Nvidia's chips decide who leads in AI. Congress wants a briefing.

13-17.q: Is he going to lose his job?
13-17.a: Not yet. He stays CEO, and the board says it backs him for now.
